chapters.title: Discernment, and letting change fuel belief

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So we're going back to this question of direct experience — having that direct experience of a teacher. And of course you can have it in a class. But are you listening, or are you activating? When you have that activation and a direct experience, that's where change happens. So the idea is: how can we activate these seeds for that change?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: People ask me, well, you really didn't explain how you did it. There are different ways — but that's why you also need a teacher. And I'm not saying follow the teacher around like you're a pet. The teacher has certain needs and wants as well, and you have to figure that out. It's a personal relationship. And what arises in you during that relationship says more about you than about the teacher. If you see things that aren't cool, you have to decide: are you going to open up your spiritual real estate to that or not?

paragraphs.speaker: Interpreter
paragraphs.text: Patrimonio espiritual.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I like that word. That's cool. So it's your discernment. You have to think: is this relationship working or not working?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And it's really up to you to do the work. It's a hard reality, actually. But once you connect with it — when you finally start seeing those changes — the changes will fuel your belief. That was a question last night. That's how belief happens. Belief doesn't happen by wishing it to happen. If you see the change, and experience it, and arise as a different person — then you'll believe it. When I look back at young Tim, I go — wow, okay, there's been a lot of change. Am I perfect yet? By no means. But I can see the difference. I'm like, okay, this works for me.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So, slide number four, Gina.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: What's the first thing you need to be able to change? Next slide. Wow, we're having some weird tech obstacles tonight. Next one.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Okay — what do we need? {audience answers} That's not the word I'm looking for. Safety. We need to experience safety first.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: There's a whole field of study about nervous system regulation. It is vast and expansive. And we're learning so much about how the human body works.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: In order to have change, the first thing we need is to feel safe to change. Because if we don't feel safe, all of those scripts, or stories, or beliefs, are just going to keep reasserting themselves. Because you're going to arise in fear. You are that fear. Or that worry. Or that anxiety. And how you handle anxiety or fear or worry is a pattern you've probably had since you were very small.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And if you're constantly in that state, to be able to change is very hard. So the first seed to think about is: how do I find safety? How can I feel comfortable in my own skin?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And this is leisure and fortune. Okay, Lam Rim people — steps on the path. In order to progress up those stages, there has to be a kind of safety. So, my team — if you're trying to teach leisure and fortune to new people, you could talk about how lucky you are to be born as a human, how lucky you are to actually be able to be in Casa Tartuk right now — irrespective of whatever's going on in your life, or how difficult things are, or how you view yourself. All the things I talked about, like the old Tim used to think of himself. There's all this leisure and fortune around this.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But until you feel safe, change is so difficult. Why do you think the five goals of DCI begin with money, relationships, and health? Because if you don't have some semblance of those three things, you're going to be living in a world of stress, a world of anxiety, a lack of safety. Now, how you relate to those things is also part of the path too, right?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: You can't take the money with you, I'm sorry. They can shove it into your coffin with you. If you want, they can burn it with your body when you get cremated.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: There's this beautiful tomb in Xi'an, China. An emperor from the seventh or eighth century — a long time ago — built himself a tomb, a secret tomb, exquisite, ornate. He hired the best artists of China of the time. And then he killed them all, so nobody knew where the tomb was. And so he's buried there. Riches, wealth, everything. It's a beautiful tomb. You actually can't go in it, but they put cameras in it, and you can wear virtual reality glasses and walk around. It's incredible. The technology, and the preservation of history, is extraordinary. But the gold is still there. He's long gone, but the riches are still there.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So when we talk about money and safety — you've got to have a different relationship with it too. But safety is where we need to start. And how do you get that? We're going to talk about that now.

chapters.title: Looking inward at what makes us feel unsafe

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: It's not just easy to be like, oh, plant this seed. It is easy, but not easy — like, help other people feel safe, help other people feel comfortable. You can do all those things, and you should. But I want to go at it from a different angle tonight, where we learn to look at the things that make us feel unsafe. The things that are in us — that are in me. The relationship we have with them is a lack of safety. Same seed — you're experiencing it as a lack of safety. That's in you.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So if we identify what some of those things are, and then learn to plant the seeds around those things, it's an investigation into you — with the goal of being able to change. Not to judge ourselves. Not, "oh my God, I'm such a terrible person, I've been like this my whole life." You have been — sorry. But if you're here, you probably have a motivation to change. And it's difficult sometimes. Sometimes we need to go into the depths of it to come out of it. But it doesn't have to be painful either, if we can look at it with an understanding of why — why did it show up in the first place? It showed up because you planted something else in the past.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I was talking to Ale earlier about this. And the whole idea is that a lot of these patterns we're going to look at — this is not a solve-every-problem-tonight thing — a lot of these took shape in our childhood. They took shape then, and then we continued them onwards. We don't have to worry about why. Sometimes things happen. Some things are sometimes difficult and very strong, and they also shaped who you are. And so if those things are still within you, they're going to stop you from advancing, because there's some kind of friction. It's like sandpaper. And it's so deep within us that we don't even recognize we're perpetuating that feeling, that experience, over and over again. If you're not aware of this lack of safety and how it appears in your life, we're subconsciously just planting those seeds over and over.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So that's one aspect. The other part is that we don't want to focus on it like we're going to spend ten years in talk therapy about it. We want to blow through those things quickly too. We don't want to diminish their importance, but at the same time, we need to understand why, so we can change it.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And this is where tartuking comes in as a main force. We have to balance all of this work with rejoicing. Because it's very easy to get stuck in the narratives — "I'm so evolved, because I'm so aware of my triggers." You know people like this, and they can tell you every single story about why they do what they do. "That's my trigger. That's my boundary. Don't do that." It's like what the kids are doing these days — they're learning to communicate about it. But do you want to be triggered, or do you want to not be triggered? I don't even want the trigger to be there in the first place.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So that's a kind of nirvana. It's an absence — an absence of the thing that caused your mental affliction, the absence of the thing that's causing a negativity. An arhat doesn't get upset. It doesn't matter what happens — you can cut off their fingers and they're like, oh, that hurts, but it doesn't turn into a negativity. Wouldn't it be cool to just not get upset, or have any kind of negative reaction to things? And I'm not even talking outwards, I'm talking inwards. I think a lot of us are pretty good with the outwards. Some of us are good. Some of us have our moments. But it's that inner critic. That inner voice.
